title: Manna and Water from the Rock
lead: God cares for His people on the long road, too. Even in the desert He provides springs.
questions: What is my daily manna that I’ve stopped noticing because it falls every morning?
Whose hands has God used to feed you over the past few months, and have you called it what it is?
Who could you be manna for this week, the ordinary-looking kind: a meal, a phone call, a ride?
note: Scripture quotations are from the Berean Standard Bible (public domain) unless otherwise noted.

paragraphs: Three days passed between the song by the sea and the first grumbling. Most of life doesn’t happen beside a parting sea; it happens on the road, where you have to eat something every day. In the wilderness the hungry people said a sentence that is a masterpiece of selective memory: if only we had died in Egypt, where “we sat by pots of meat.” From the country where their sons had been drowned, what they remembered was the pots. Israel got out of Egypt in one night. It took forty years to get Egypt out of Israel.

The most astonishing thing is God’s answer: He didn’t respond to the grumbling with punishment but with food. “I will rain down bread from heaven for you.” In the morning something lay on the desert floor, “as fine as frost on the ground,” and the people asked, “What is it?” The question became the gift’s name. Manna taught God’s economy: an omer per person, and “he who gathered much had no excess, and he who gathered little had no shortfall.” What some tried to store up went bad by morning. The trust God was teaching through the manna had a shelf life of one day and had to be renewed every morning. The prayer Jesus would later teach reflects the same rhythm: give us this day our daily bread. The Sabbath was part of that rhythm, too, even before Sinai: on the sixth day they gathered a double portion, which, for once, didn’t spoil and was still fresh on the seventh day. God taught rest through the way He served the food.

At Rephidim, when the water ran out, the question came: “Is the LORD among us or not?” After the plagues, after the sea, after the manna. God didn’t answer with an argument but with a gift, and what a gift: “I will stand before you there on the rock in Horeb. You shall strike the rock, and water will come out of it” (WEB). The blow of the staff fell where God was standing, and from the struck place came life for the guilty. Centuries later Paul would add: “and that rock was Christ.” Manna fell for the entire forty years, including all the years of punishment for rebellion. God doesn’t take back breakfast because of yesterday’s rebellion. His everyday faithfulness makes no noise: it looks like frost on the ground, like an ordinary day when nothing ran short.

Three days passed between the song of joy by the sea and the first grumbling. That’s how long the fresh memory of the greatest miracle in Israel’s history lasted: three days of marching without water. Then came the bitter water at Marah, after that the Desert of Sin and hunger, and after that Rephidim and thirst. This stretch of the road has none of the drama of the sea. It is as monotonous as the desert itself: another day, another shortage, another complaint. And that is exactly why it matters so much. Most of life doesn’t happen beside a parting sea. It happens on the road, where you have to eat something every day.

sections.heading: A Log in Bitter Water
paragraphs: The first stop in God’s school for Israel was called Marah, which means Bitterness. After three days without water they finally found a spring, but “they could not drink the water there because it was bitter.” It’s hard to imagine a sharper disappointment. False hope of meeting a burning need was worse than no water at all. “And Moses cried out to the LORD, and the LORD showed him a log. And when he cast it into the waters, they were sweetened.” God didn’t point them to another spring. He healed the one that was there. Sometimes God doesn’t lead us to a new well; He sweetens the bitter water we’re standing beside: the same marriage, the same church, the same job. The narrator adds one more line here about God testing Israel. Marah wasn’t an accident along the route. It was the first lesson.

sections.heading: Pots of Meat
paragraphs: In the Desert of Sin, the hungry people say a sentence that is a masterpiece of selective memory: “If only we had died by the LORD’s hand in the land of Egypt!… There we sat by pots of meat and ate our fill of bread.” By pots of meat. From the country where their sons had been drowned, where they had to meet their brick quota without being given straw, what they remembered was the pots. Hunger has a way of repainting the past: slavery seen from an empty stomach looks like prosperity, and the house of bondage looks like home. Israel got out of Egypt in one night. It took forty years to get Egypt out of Israel. Anyone who has left some Egypt behind knows that voice: at least back there you knew what was for dinner. In our memories, the old life always shows us the menu, never the bill. That is why the decision to leave can’t be made just once; on a long road you have to make it again at every empty pot.

sections.heading: Bread Raining from Heaven
paragraphs: The most astonishing thing in this scene is God’s answer. To the grumbling, the idealizing of slavery, the open ingratitude, God doesn’t respond with punishment or a lecture. He responds with food: “I will rain down bread from heaven for you.” In the morning, when the dew had lifted, “there were thin flakes on the desert floor, as fine as frost on the ground.” The Israelites asked one another, “What is it?” because they didn’t know what it was, and the question stuck to the gift as its name. Manna means “What is it?” For forty years Israel would live every day on something they couldn’t name. It “tasted like wafers made with honey,” and it came with a monotony that was itself a message: every morning, without a break, no matter what mood the people had been in the day before. That same evening, quail had flown in and covered the camp; they got the meat they had been shouting for, too. God answered the menu of their complaints point by point, as if to show that He doesn’t take offense at the way a hungry person asks. God’s faithfulness can be as spectacular as a split sea, but on an ordinary day it looks like frost on the ground: small, quiet, and easy to miss.

sections.heading: An Omer per Person
paragraphs: The rules for gathering manna hold the whole economy of God’s gift: “Each one is to gather as much as he needs. You may take an omer for each person.” And then a sentence that sounds like a smaller miracle than the sea, though maybe a harder one: “he who gathered much had no excess, and he who gathered little had no shortfall.” With manna, you couldn’t build up an advantage. You couldn’t stockpile at your neighbor’s expense, because whatever was kept until morning “became infested with maggots and began to smell.” The gift was measured for today and for everyone. Centuries later Paul would quote that sentence to the churches, teaching them to share with those who had less: with God, some people’s surplus exists to cover other people’s shortfall. And the prayer Jesus would teach reflects the rhythm of the manna: give us this day our daily bread. This day. Not next week. The trust God was teaching through the manna had a shelf life of one day and had to be renewed every morning.

sections.heading: The School of the Sabbath
paragraphs: The manna brought one more lesson, delivered without a single word of lecture. On the sixth day the people gathered a double portion, and the part that would have spoiled on any other night was fresh on the seventh day: “it did not smell or contain any maggots.” On the seventh day, no manna fell. God taught the Sabbath through the way He served the food: six days of gathering, and on the seventh, food from a supply that, for once, didn’t go bad. Notice that this happened before the Sabbath commandment was given at Sinai. Rest on the seventh day didn’t begin with an order carved in stone. It began with the rhythm in which God fed His people, and with the creation in which He Himself rested. The law only put a name to what grace had been doing for a long time.

sections.heading: A Jar to Remember
paragraphs: There is one more instruction in this chapter, given as if ahead of its time: “Take a jar and fill it with an omer of manna. Then place it before the LORD to be preserved for the generations to come.” One omer, one person’s daily ration, was to be kept for generations, “so that they may see the bread I fed you in the wilderness.” God had them preserve evidence of His daily faithfulness, because He knew future generations would know manna only from stories, and it’s easy to doubt stories about somebody else’s desert. It’s worth having a jar like that in your own life: an experience written down, a date, a keepsake from that year when it shouldn’t have been enough, and it was. Remembering yesterday’s bread can’t replace today’s trust, but without that memory today’s trust has nothing to stand on.

sections.heading: Is the LORD Among Us or Not?
paragraphs: At Rephidim the water ran out, and so did the politeness: “the people contended with Moses,” and Moses cried out to God, “A little more and they will stone me!” God’s answer contains a detail that’s easy to overlook: “I will stand before you there on the rock in Horeb. You shall strike the rock, and water will come out of it” (WEB). The Lord stands on the rock that the staff is about to strike. With that same staff Moses had struck the Nile, turning Egypt’s water into blood, and now he strikes the place where God is standing. The result: water flows from the rock for a grumbling people. The instrument of judgment is used for a gift, and the blow falls where the Lord stands. The place got a double name, Massah and Meribah, testing and quarreling, and the narrator recorded the question asked there: “Is the LORD among us or not?” That question comes after ten plagues, after the Passover night, after the split sea, after the manna and the quail. That is what human memory is like when it comes to miracles: yesterday’s bread doesn’t satisfy today’s thirst. And that is why God answers the question not with an argument but with another gift. Massah and Meribah didn’t disappear from the Bible along with that generation. Centuries later the psalmist would warn, “do not harden your hearts as you did at Meribah, in the day at Massah in the wilderness.” And Paul would look at this scene even more deeply and write of Israel in the wilderness that they drank from the spiritual rock that went with them, “and that rock was Christ.” The blow that fell on the place where God stood, and brought out water for the guilty, turned out to be a preview of something greater. There is Someone who takes the blows meant for others, and from His wounds flows life.

sections.heading: Forty Years
paragraphs: There is one more sentence in this chapter, quiet and enormous: “The Israelites ate manna forty years, until they came to a land where they could settle.” Forty years is longer than planned. Most of those years were punishment for a rebellion we’ll read about tomorrow; the generation that refused to believe wandered the wilderness until it died out. But the manna kept falling in those years, too. Every day, through all the years of punishment, the same bread as before fell on a camp of people who had thrown away their chance. God doesn’t feed only the obedient, and He doesn’t take back breakfast because of yesterday’s rebellion. Centuries later, in another wilderness, a hungry Man would answer the tempter with the words Moses used to sum up the lesson of the manna: man does not live on bread alone. And then He would say of Himself: I am the bread of life. The manna pointed ahead to the meeting of our deepest need, which is rescue, and He is the answer to the question “What is it?”

sections.heading: For Today
paragraphs: Yesterday’s reading was about the sea; today’s is about breakfast, and that is a good order, because those are the proportions of life. Great deliverances are rare; you need food every day. This story says that God is present in both: the One who splits the sea also measures out an omer per person. If you are on a long, monotonous road where nothing changes but the date, then the manna is good news for you in particular: God’s faithfulness doesn’t show itself in fireworks, but in the fact that every morning there is something to eat. One question is worth asking yourself straight out: can I recognize today’s manna, or do I miss it because it looks too ordinary, like frost on the ground, like an ordinary day when nothing ran short? In a church community, manna rarely looks like a miracle either. It looks like someone who drives an older sister to worship every week, like a meal brought over after a funeral, like a phone call to someone at just the right time. God’s care for people on a long road usually has someone’s hands and someone’s car, and maybe that is exactly why it’s so easy to chalk it up to chance.
